promptLatex: In a group of 70 students, 35 take math, 30 take physics, and 20 take chemistry. 12 take both math and physics, 8 take both math and chemistry, and 5 take both physics and chemistry. 3 take all three subjects. How many students take exactly one subject?
hintLatex: Count the exclusive regions directly, rather than the total and subtracting.
For one subject, subtract the two pairwise intersections from its headcount and add the triple intersection back: only math is $35 - 12 - 8 + 3 = 18$.
Only physics is $30 - 12 - 5 + 3 = 16$ and only chemistry is $20 - 8 - 5 + 3 = 10$, so the three regions hold $18 + 16 + 10 = 44$ students.
solutionLatex:
Count each exclusive region separately, being careful not to double-count the students in more than one subject.

Only math: $35 - 12 - 8 + 3 = 18$. The $+3$ puts back the students that the two pairwise subtractions each removed.

Only physics: $30 - 12 - 5 + 3 = 16$.

Only chemistry: $20 - 8 - 5 + 3 = 10$.

Students taking exactly one subject: $18 + 16 + 10 = 44$.

As a check, exactly two is $(12-3) + (8-3) + (5-3) = 16$ and all three is $3$, so $44 + 16 + 3 = 63$ students take at least one subject and the remaining $70 - 63 = 7$ take none.
